strengths: Presents the first systematic study of quantization-aware training (QAT) specifically tailored for the fused FlashAttention operator, addressing a major blocker for end-to-end FP4 inference on modern GPUs.

Identifies and mathematically resolves the subtle precision mismatches in FlashAttention's backward pass (i.e., the mismatch of attention score recomputation and the breakdown of the $P^\top dP = dO^\top O$ identity under quantization).

Demonstrates strong empirical performance across competitive generative models, including state-of-the-art video diffusion models (Wan 2.1 14B) and LLMs (Llama 3.1 70B), effectively recovering BF16 quality without complex runtime outlier mitigation.
Achieves notable speedups of up to 1.5x on the RTX 5090 compared to SageAttention3, since QAT allows the removal of expensive preprocessing overheads like Q/K smoothing during inference.
weaknesses: Requires storing an additional high-precision output tensor ($O'$) during the forward pass for backward recomputation, which increases the training memory footprint and necessitates gradient checkpointing.
The performance benefits of the custom kernels are highly dependent on Blackwell architecture GPUs (such as RTX 5090, B200), with older architectures relying on slower emulation.
There is a minor inconsistency in the text: Appendix B.2 (page 13) mentions running continued training experiments on 'Qwen3-8B', whereas Table 3 and Table 4 report results for 'Qwen3-14B'.

strengths: Provides the first systematic and technically detailed study of 4-bit Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) for the attention mechanism.

Identifies the core mathematical and precision-related reasons why naive QAT fails with FlashAttention-style recomputation (such as the breaking of the $P^\top dP = dO^\top O$ identity due to mixed-precision, and mismatch in $P$ precision during backward pass).

Proposes elegant, principled modifications to the forward and backward passes (computing an auxiliary high-precision $O'$ and fake-quantizing $P$ in the backward pass) that ensure mathematical consistency and training stability.

Achieves excellent empirical results, recovering almost all the quality drop on diffusion models (Wan 2.1) and large language models (Qwen-3 14B) without requiring complex, performance-degrading post-training quantization heuristics like those in SageAttention3.
Demonstrates strong inference speedups (1.1x–1.5x) on Blackwell-based hardware (RTX 5090) compared to SageAttention3 by avoiding outlier-mitigation pre-processing overhead.
weaknesses: The requirement to compute and store a high-precision output $O'$ during the forward pass increases memory pressure during training, necessitating full gradient checkpointing to avoid Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors as mentioned in the Appendix.

The recovery of accuracy on the largest model evaluated (Llama 3.1 70B) is only partial compared to the BF16 baseline. Although the authors note this is due to training budget constraints, it highlights that scaling QAT to very large models remains challenging.
There are minor inconsistencies and typos in the manuscript: for instance, Appendix B.2 repeatedly refers to 'Qwen3-8B' while the main text and Tables 3 and 4 evaluate 'Qwen3-14B'.

strengths: Identifies a highly critical and subtle mathematical inconsistency when naively applying Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) to FlashAttention: specifically, how the fundamental algebraic identity $P^T dP = dO^T O$ breaks when the output $O$ is computed in low precision (FP4) while gradients are computed in high precision (BF16).

Proposes an elegant and effective solution to compute and store a high-precision auxiliary output $O'$ during the forward pass, restoring training stability and eliminating gradient explosion without requiring complex post-training heuristic smoothing.

Provides a strong, multi-modal empirical evaluation, demonstrating successful recovery of model quality on challenging tasks like video diffusion (Wan 2.1 1.3B/14B) and large language models (Qwen-3 14B, Llama 3.1 70B).
Delivers real hardware execution speedups (1.1x to 1.5x over SageAttention3) on Blackwell architecture (RTX 5090) by removing the runtime overhead of outlier mitigation techniques during inference.
weaknesses: The memory footprint of the training kernel is increased because it requires storing an extra high-precision output buffer $O'$ and keeping extra buffers for fake-quantized inputs, forcing the use of activation checkpointing and sharding to avoid Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. A detailed memory overhead analysis is missing.

A direct comparison of throughput and accuracy against SageAttention3 during inference must be contextualized by the significant computational cost of the QAT phase (e.g., hours of training on multiple H200/B200 GPUs), which is not required by Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) methods.
The study is highly hardware-specific, focusing primarily on Blackwell NVFP4 format, which limits its immediate applicability to older or non-NVIDIA hardware platforms.

There are minor presentation issues, such as referencing 'Qwen-3 14B' which appears to be a very recent or potentially unreleased model, without sufficient explanation of its architecture relative to standard benchmarks.
